Therefore, it finds wide range of applications such as actuators, sensors, transducers, hydrophones, information technology, robotics and biomedical engineering etc.. Researchers worldwide are in search of safer lead free piezo materials as an alternative to toxic lead (Pb) bearing PZT. Some lead free piezo systems explored so far are: (i) Bismuth Sodium Titanate (BNT), (ii) Bismuth Potassium Titanate (BKT), (iii) Sodium Potassium Niobium (NKN), (iv) Potassium Sodium Niobate (KNN), and (v) Barium Titanate (BaTiO3) etc. The main drawbacks of alkali (Na, K) based lead-free piezo ceramics are low d 33, difficult in maintaining stoichiometry due to high volatilization and corrosive at high temperature. Barium Titanate (BT) and BT modified materials are promising due to high d 33 associated with composition-induced transitions such as morphotropic phase boundary (MPB) or polymorphic phase transitions (PPT). Barium Titanate (BT) has been modified as Barium Zirconate Titanate (BZT) by addition of zirconia, which influences the crystal structure and electrical properties. Wang et al. synthesized CaE^{2+} and ZrE^{4+} co-doped BT material with exceptionally high piezoelectric charge constant by optimization of calcination and sintering temperature. The effect of various dopants such as CeE^{4+}, YE^{3+}, HoE^{3+} and CaE^{2+} on a BZT system has been studied. The dielectric and microstructure properties of MgE^{2+} doped BT , relaxor behavior of MgE^{2+} doped BZT and SrE^{2+} doped BZT have already been studied. However, a comparative study on effect of various dopants on electrical properties such as ferroelectric and piezoelectric properties of BZT is not reported. The large strain response with good temperature stability would be quite suitable for environmental-friendly solid-state actuator applications."," Lead-based ferroelectric materials such as lead zirconate titanate (PZT) have been widely utilized for piezoelectric or dielectric components and other electromechanical devices. Nevertheless, the large amounts of hazardous lead in these materials have spurred enormous efforts to search for new alternate lead-free materials. Since the bismuth-based perovskite ceramics, Bi1/2Na1/2TiO3 (BNT) was found to possess promising piezoelectric and ferroelectric properties, various promising BNT-based solid solutions have been proposed: examples including the binary Bi1/2Na1/2TiO3-BaTiO3 (BNT-BT) , Bi1/2Na1/2TiO3-K0.5Na0.5NbO3 (BNT-KNN) , the ternary Bi1/2Na1/2TiO3-Bi1/2K1/2TiO3-BaTiO3 (BNT-BKT-BT) , Bi1/2Na1/2TiO3-BaTiO3-(K0.5Na0.5)NbO3 (BNT-BT-KNN) and Bi1/2Na1/2TiO3-BaTiO3-BiAlO3 (BNT-BT-BA). Although extensive efforts have been done in lead-free alternatives, the lead-free counterparts still cannot compete with the lead-based ones in terms of the global electrical properties. There is an urgent demand to develop new piezoelectric lead-free materials with desired properties. Zhang et al. reported a Bi1/2Na1/2TiO3-BaTiO3-K0.5Na0.5NbO3 (BNT-BT-KNN) ceramics having a giant strain response of 0.45% at 80kV/cm driving field equivalently 560pm/V. Pham et al. studied a Nb-doped Bi1/2(Na0.82K0.18)1/2TiO3 (BNKTN) ceramics near the morphotropic phase boundary (MPB) and reported a large unipolar strain of 0.448% at 70kV/cm. The subsequent researches on the mechanism of the giant strain in BNT-based systems, as well as new BNT-based compositions further accelerated studies on BNT-based ceramics. However, the practical application of BNT-based ceramics is hindered due to the fact that large strain response needs a high electric field to trigger. In previous work, most of the studies were focused on the A-site substitution or B-site single-ion replacement, while little attention has been paid to the effect of B-site complex ions substitution. Jin et al. introduced (Al0.5Nb0.5)E^{4+} into the B-site of BNT and found a large strain S max/E max of 575pm/V and high piezoelectric constant d33 of 210 pC/N. Li et al. prepared Fe-modified 0.875Bi0.5Na0.5TiO3-0.06Bi0.5Li0.5TiO3-0.065BaTiO3-0.005Mn ceramic with a large unipolar strain of 0.4% under 40kV/cm. In light of these observations, a new ternary solid solution was designed and characterized through introducing B-site complex-ion (Fe1/2Nb1/2)E^{4+} into the MPB solid solution (Bi1/2Na1/2)0.935Ba0.065TiO3 (BNBT). It is expected that (Fe1/2Nb1/2)E^{4+} modification in BNBT ceramics can enhance the electromechanical properties. In this work, we fabricated BNBT-based ceramics with (Fe1/2Nb1/2)E^{4+} addition using a conventional solid-state reaction method and systematically studied the influence of compositional modification on the crystal structure, ferroelectric and piezoelectric properties and field-induced strain behaviors."," The (Bi1/2Na1/2)0.935Ba0.065Ti1\u2212x (Fe1/2Nb1/2)xO3 (BNBT-x FN)(x =0.000, 0.005, 0.010, 0.015, 0.020, 0.030) ceramics were prepared by the conventional solid-state reaction method using reagent-grade metal oxides or carbonate powders of Bi2O3 (99%), TiO2 (99.5%), Na2CO3 (99.8%), BaCO3 (99%), Fe2O3 (99.49%) and Nb2O5 (99.96%) as starting materials. All raw materials were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. The raw materials were weighed at stoichiometric proportion and then mixed homogenised by planetary ball milling in a polyethylene with stabilized zirconia balls for 12h, using anhydrous ethanol as liquid medium. After drying, the mixed powders were calcined at 850\xb0C for 2h and then milled again for 6h. Then the powders were mixed with an appropriate amount of polyvinyl butyral (PVB) binder, and pressed into pallets having a diameter of 12mm and a thickness of 1.0mm under the pressure of about 200MPa. After burning off PVB, the ceramics were sintered in an alumina crucible at 1100\u20131180\xb0C for 2h in air. To avoid the loss of bismuth and sodium oxides during sintering, the pellets were embedded into preprepared powder with the same composition. The crystal structure of the ceramics was determined by X-ray diffraction (XRD) using a Cu K\u03b1 radiation (\u03bb =1.54178\xc5) (D8 Advance, Bruker Inc., Germany). The microstructure of the ceramics was observed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (JSM-6380, Japan) on polished and thermally etched cross-sections as well as on fracture surfaces. The density of the ceramics was analyzed using electronic densimeter (MatsuHaku, QL-300C, Taiwan). Silver electrodes were coated on the top and bottom surfaces of the ceramics for the subsequent electrical measurements. The ferroelectric hysteresis loops, bipolar and unipolar strain curves were measured, at 10Hz in silicon oil with the aid of a Sawyer\u2013Tower circuit to apply an electric field with sinusoidal waveform, with ferroelectric analyzer (TF2000 analyzer, Aixacct, Germany) along with the laser interferometer (SIOS Me\xdftechnik GmbH, Germany) under an electric field of 50kV/cm. The samples were poled in silicon oil at room temperature under 50\u201370kV/cm for 20min, and piezoelectric measurements were then carried out using a quasi-static d33 -meter YE2730 (SINOCERA, China). The temperature dependence of dielectric properties was measured by a broadband dielectric spectrometer (Novocontrol Germany) at temperatures ranging from room temperature to 500\xb0C with a heating rate of 3\xb0C/min.",," The XRD patterns with a 2\u03b8 ranging from 20\xb0 to 70\xb0 for BNBT-x FN samples are demonstrated in (a). All ceramics exhibited a pure perovskite structure and no second phases or impurities can be observed. This implied that the doped (Fe1/2Nb1/2)E^{4+} have diffused into the crystal lattice and formed a stable solid solution with BNBT. (b) shows the expanded XRD patterns in the 2\u03b8 range of 45\u201348\xb0. The positions of (202) peak shift slightly to the lower angle with the increase of (Fe1/2Nb1/2)E^{4+} content, suggesting the expansion of lattice constant. This was attributed to the differences in ionic radii of FeE^{3+} (0.645\xc5, CN=6), NbE^{5+} (0.64\xc5, CN=6) and TiE^{4+} (0.605\xc5, CN=6) , The results indicated that the (Fe1/2Nb1/2)E^{4+} is entered into the B-site of BNT to substitute TiE^{4+} for the radius matching, while the differences in ionic radii resulting in the lattice deformation at the same time. The similar observations were also reported in previous studies. The XRD data were collected in a 2\u03b8 range of 20\u201380\xb0 with a step size of 0.02\xb0. The final refined profiles for BNBT and BNBT-0.020FN are presented in. A change in the shape of P\u2013E loops from \u201cslim\u201d to \u201cwell-saturated\u201d implies that the domain structure of the ceramics undergoes a macrodomain\u2013microdomain transition with the increasing (Fe1/2Nb1/2)E^{4+} amount, which also confirms the appearance of a typical relaxor behavior at high doping level of (Fe1/2Nb1/2)E^{4+} ( \u22650.020). The compositionally induced ferroelectric to relaxor-ferroelectric phase transformation can be well verified by the bipolar strain measurements (see ). Pure BNBT ceramic exhibits a typical butterfly-shaped curve with a maximum strain (S max) of 0.18% and negative strain (S neg) of 0.06%, which is typical for ferroelectric material. The field-induced strain and the corresponding normalized strain of BNBT-x FN ceramic and some other lead-free BNT-based systems are summarized in for reference. It is clear that (Fe1/2Nb1/2)E^{4+} is of benefit to the ferroelectric and piezoelectric properties of BNT-based ceramics. The temperature dependence of the strains should be a key feature for actuator systems since the strain fluctuation would degrade the positioning accuracy. Electric field dependence of the relative dielectric constant of BNBT-x FN ceramics is manifested in. Compositions with x <0.020 exhibit evident hysteretic behavior, which is closely connected to switching of ferroelectric domains. Before the coercive field is reached, the domain wall density increases, and hence permittivity increases as well. Owing to the stress that is associated with the strain incompatibility of switching domains, clamping occurs, which leads to a decrease of permittivity. In addition, the number of domain walls diminishes at high field, and therefore hysteresis becomes smaller at higher fields. On the contrary, BNBT-x FN samples (x \u22650.02) display indiscernible hysteretic behavior, implying little domain switching. Judging from the evolution of \u03f5r (E), it is evident that compositions with x =0.02 and x =0.03 keep permittivity high as in the undoped BNBT at zero electric field. In addition, it reduces the effect of the electric bias field on the permittivity, so that the relative deviation calculated through the maximum permittivity \u03f5 max, the minimum permittivity \u03f5 min, and the permittivity at zero field \u03f5 0kV according to Eq. changes from 47% (x =0) to 50% (x =0.005), 65% (x =0.010), 64% (x =0.015), 40% (x =0.020) and eventually to 24% (x =0.030).  shows the temperature dependence of the dielectric constant (\u03f5r ) and loss (tan \u03b4) of the BNBT-x FN ceramics with x =0.00, 0.005, 0.010, 0.015, 0.020 and 0.030 measured at different frequencies (0.1, 1, 10 and 100kHz). It is clear from the dielectric response that samples with low (Fe1/2Nb1/2)E^{4+} contents (x =0.00, 0.005 and 0.010) exhibit two anomalies commonly known as depolarization temperature (Td ) corresponding to ferroelectric-to-relaxor phase transition, and maximum temperature (Tm ), at which the dielectric constant reaches its maximum value. However, a clear change for samples x <0.015 at low temperature region with a relatively weak frequency-dependent dispersion and decreasing dielectric permittivity takes place. It is suggested that BNBT-x FN ceramics with x <0.015 are nonergodic relaxor ferroelectrics state undergoing a field-induced phase transition to a long-range ordered state, which is consistent with the previous results of BNT-BT ceramics. This means that the initially nanoscale polar regions are triggered to grow into micron-sized domains or ordered reorientation with the application of electric field. All the samples have relative low dielectric loss at room temperature. The dielectric constant decreases with increase in frequency from 0.1kHz to 100kHz. The electric field induced strains are generally correlated with domain switching, phase transition and piezoelectricity that happens in the sample driven by a high bias field. The enhancement in the field-induced strain and corresponding dE^{*} 33 is due to the distortion of (Fe1/2Nb1/2)E^{4+} entering into B-site in BNT-based ceramics. Furthermore, the relaxor ferroelectric phase dominated at higher (Fe1/2Nb1/2)E^{4+} (i.e., x =0.020 and above), which delays the transformation from the relaxor ferroelectric phase to the ferroelectric phase based on the significant decrease in the polarization response. The free energy of the ferroelectric phase was comparable to that of the relaxor ferroelectric phase under zero field, such that it can be easily induced by an external electric field and becomes saturated, as shown in. The results of this study suggest that high unipolar strain, located only in a narrow region around x =0.020 in which both ferroelectric and relaxor ferroelectric phase coexist in the BNT-based ceramics system. Beyond this narrow region, either the ferroelectric or relaxor ferroelectric phase phase dominates. Neither of the phases can solely deliver a strain as large as that measured from compositions near the boundary between polar and relaxor ferroelectric phase because this strain results from the contributions both domain switching and the field induced phase transition. The remnant polarization together with the noticeable pinched polarization hysteresis loop and large strain at x =0.020 were suggested to originate from the coexistence of the ferroelectric and relaxor ferroelectric phase. The relaxor-ferroelectric transition involves a percolation of aligned polar nanoregions, and the reverse transition involves a dissociation of randomly oriented macroscopic ferroelectric domains. The coexistence of different polarization states at the critical composition may indicate that the free energy of the ferroelectric phase seems so comparable to that of the nonpolar phase at zero fields and the nonpolar phase at a zero field can easily transform into a long-range ferroelectric phase upon the application of an electric field. d."," Pb(Zr,Ti)O3 (PZT) and PZT-based multi-component ceramics have been widely used in electromechanical devices due to their excellent piezoelectric properties. However, the strong toxicity and high volatility of lead oxide during sintering have caused severe environmental and ecological problems. Therefore, it is necessary to develop new lead-free piezoelectric ceramics. Bi0.5Na0.5TiO3 (BNT) is a perovskite-structured ferroelectric with a rhombohedral symmetry. Because of its large remanent polarization (P r =38\u03bcC/cmE^{2}), BNT has been considered as a good candidate for lead-free piezoelectric materials. However, the high coercive field (E c =7.3kV/mm) makes poling of the ceramic difficult. As a result, the BNT ceramic usually exhibits weak piezoelectric coefficient (d 33 =83pC/N) , which is significantly lower than that of the Pb(Zr0.52Ti0.48)O3 ceramic (d 33 =223pC/N). To improve the piezoelectric properties, a number of BNT-based solid solutions, such as BNT\u2013BaTiO3 , CeO2-doped BNT\u2013Bi0.5K0.5TiO3 , BNT\u2013Bi0.5K0.5TiO3\u2013KNbO3 , BNT\u2013NaNbO3 , (Bi0.5Na0.5)0.94Ba0.06Zr y Ti1\u2212 y O3 , BNT\u2013KNbO3 , BNT\u2013BaTiO3\u2013SrTiO3 , Ta-doped BNT\u2013BaTiO3 , (Bi0.5Na0.5)1+ x TiO3 , Bi0.5(Na1\u2212 x \u2212 y K x Li y )0.5TiO3 , BNT\u2013SrTiO3 and BNT\u2013Bi0.5K0.5TiO3\u2013BaTiO3 have been developed and studied intensively. Our previous works have shown that BNT\u2013BaTiO3\u2013SrTiO3 ceramics possess good piezoelectric properties and the substitution of LiE^{+} for NaE^{+} is effective in improving the piezoelectric properties and decreasing the sintering temperature of BNT-based ceramics. In the present work, a new BNT-based multi-component solid solution, (Bi0.92Na0.92\u2212 x Li x )0.5Ba0.06Sr0.02TiO3, is developed by partially substituting LiE^{+} for NaE^{+} in an A-site of 0.92BNT\u20130.06BaTiO3\u20130.02SrTiO3 ceramics. The ceramics were prepared by an ordinary sintering method, and the effects of the Li-substitution on the electrical properties (ferroelectric, piezoelectric and dielectric) of the ceramics have been investigated systematically."," A conventional ceramic fabrication technique was used to prepare the (Bi0.92Na0.92\u2212 x Li x )0.5Ba0.06Sr0.02TiO3 ceramics. Analytical-grade metal oxides and carbonate powders Bi2O3 (99%), Na2CO3 (99%), BaCO3 (99%), SrCO3 (99%), Li2CO3 (97%) and TiO2 (99.5%) were used as starting materials. The stoichiometric powders were ball-milled thoroughly in ethanol using zirconia balls for 8h, and then dried and calcined at 850\xb0C for 2h. After the calcination, the mixture was ball-milled again and mixed thoroughly with a PVA binder solution, and then pressed into disk samples. The disk samples were finally sintered at 1050\u20131200\xb0C for 2h in air. Silver electrodes were fired on both surfaces of the samples for the subsequent poling and measurements. The samples were poled under a dc field of 5\u20137kV/mm at room temperature in a silicone oil bath for 30min. The crystalline structure of the sintered samples was examined using X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis with Cu K\u03b1 radiation (\u03bb =0.154nm, DX-1000). The microstructures were observed using scanning electron microscopy (JEOL JSM-5900LV). The density of the ceramics was measured by the Archimedes method. The relative permittivity \u03b5 r and loss tangent tan \u03b4 of the ceramics at 1kHz, 10kHz and 100kHz were measured as functions of temperature using an impedance analyzer (Agilent 4192A). A conventional Sawyer\u2013Tower circuit was used to measure the polarization hysteresis (P\u2013E) loop at 50Hz. The electromechanical coupling factors k p and k t were determined by the resonance method according to the IEEE Standard using an impedance analyzer (Agilent 4294A). However, they produce harmful materials, such as Pb x O y (PbO, PbO2), during production and usage process. These harmful materials could cause huge damage to the human body and environment. BaTiO3 (BT) ceramics are one of the important parts of lead-free piezoelectric ceramics, and they are the first perovskite piezoelectric material applied in practice. Therefore, researchers pay much attention on BT ceramics for replacing PZT ceramics. However, the developments of BT ceramics are limited by inferior electrical properties and low Curie temperature. Therefore, researchers want to improve the performance of BT ceramics through various means. In 2009, Liu et al.  synthesised Ba(Ti0\xb78Zr0.2)O3-(Ba0\xb77Ca0.3)TiO3 ceramics by Ca/Zr co-doping and successfully constructed a morphotropic phase boundary to achieve excellent electrical properties. Improvements in densification and piezoelectric properties have been observed for potassium sodium niobate system modified with LiNbO3 , LiTaO3 , SrTiO3 , BiFeO3 , LiSbO3 and CaTiO3. Among the potassium sodium niobate based contenders, the composition K0.5Na0.5NbO3 (KNN) has been paid much attention since the discovery of KNN-based textured ceramics with properties comparable to those of unmodified PZT ceramics. This work provides a new insight into the improvement of Bi1/2Na1/2TiO3-based lead-free piezoelectric ceramics."," For more than half a century, lead-based piezoelectrics, such as Pb(Zr, Ti)O3 (PZT), Pb(Mg1/3Nb2/3)O3-PbTiO3 (PMN-PT), etc., have been widely used in various types of piezoelectric devices, due to their excellent piezoelectric properties and good thermal stability. However, these lead-based materials are facing global restrictions, because the toxic Pb may cause serious problems concerned with both human health and environment. Therefore, it is urgent to search for the lead-free alternatives. Bi1/2Na1/2TiO3 (BNT)-based ceramics are expected to be one of the most promising lead-free candidates because of the superior piezoelectric property. The giant electric-field-induced strains discovered in BNT-based ceramics have further attracted considerable interests in the past few years. Unfortunately, the piezoelectric thermal stability of BNT-based ceramics is poor. Although they possess a high maximum dielectric constant temperature (T m ~ 300\xb0C), their depolarization temperature (T d), at which piezoelectric properties degrade, is usually far below T m. Devices utilizing small-signal piezoelectric properties, such as non-resonance piezoelectric sensors and energy harvesters, require ceramics with large piezoelectric constants and the good thermal stability. Thus, the low T d is the main drawback of BNT-based ceramics for these kinds of applications. It is of great importance to explore methods to promote depolarization temperature and further improve piezoelectric properties of BNT-based ceramics. There are currently two approaches to tailor the thermal depolarization behavior of BNT-based materials. One approach is forming ferroelectric/semiconductor composites. It is reported recently that piezoelectric thermal stability is significantly enhanced by introducing ZnO to form BNT-based piezoceramic composites. However, the piezoceramic composite is hard to fabricate; the sintering process should be very carefully controlled to ensure the densification of the material and to prevent the diffusion between the semiconductor and ferroelectric phases. Another approach is substitutional modification, which is more facile to fabricate than piezoceramic composites. For a long time, it is believed that there is an inverse relationship between d 33 and T d in BNT-based systems with substitutional modifications. For example, by adding tetragonal Bi1/2K1/2TiO3 (BKT) into the rhombohedral BNT, the piezoelectric properties are significantly improved due to the formation of morphotropic phase boundary (MPB) , whereas the depolarization temperature decreases rapidly down in the vicinity of MPB. As another example, Mn doping in 0.96BNT-0.04BiAlO3 was found to increase T d but decrease d 33. This inverse relationship between d 33 and T d used to be understood in terms of the stability of domain configuration , where higher T d means more stable domains, thus the contributions from domain wall motion are suppressed, consequently the d 33 decreases. However, recent studies call for a new insight into the relationship between d 33 and T d. Simultaneous reduction of both d 33 and T d was observed in BNT-BKT ceramics modified by (K,Na)NbO3 (KNN) , BiMeO3 (Me = Al, Sc, Mn) , and ZrE^{4+} , which implies that the inverse relationship between d 33 and T d cannot be a universal rule in BNT-based systems. The reduction of both d 33 and T d was found to be due to the disruption of long-range ferroelectric order. This founding reminds us the possibility of simultaneous improvement of d 33 and T d by stabilizing of ferroelectric order. In our previous work, a stabilization effect on the long-range ferroelectric order in Bi1/2(Na0.8K0.2)1/2TiO3 (BNKT, the MPB composition) by Fe doping was found. It is thus interesting to verify whether Fe doping can simultaneously improve the piezoelectric property and thermal stability. In this study, the effect of Fe doping on piezoelectric property and depolarization behavior of BNKT lead-free ceramics is investigated. The results show that Fe doping at an appropriate level improves both piezoelectric constant d 33 and depolarization temperature T d simultaneously. Thus, in turn, by stabilizing the long-range ferroelectric order, the piezoelectric property and thermal stability is likely to be simultaneously improved in a BNT-based system with obvious relaxor character. Piezoelectric ceramics with both high piezoelectric property and good thermal stability are demanded by practical applications. In the present study, we have demonstrated that stabilization of the long-range ferroelectric order in BNKT by Fe doping leads to simultaneous improvement of both piezoelectric property and thermal stability. We believe that this effect may be also applicable to other similar material systems, and could be provided as a guidance for further improving performance of BNT-based materials for piezoelectric applications.
